article_content: Sudan's ruling military council has declared it is discontinuing all negotiations with civilian protesters following a devastating military operation that left over 100 protesters dead in Khartoum. General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan stated in a televised address that a new government will be formed immediately, without input from protest groups, and will remain in power until elections are held under international supervision within nine months. The military's decision comes after the collapse of talks with the Alliance for Freedom and Change, a coalition of protesters and opposition parties. The Sudanese Professionals Association described Monday's attack as a 'massacre,' accusing security forces of indiscriminate violence. Tibor Nagy, the top U.S. diplomat to Africa, sharply condemned the attack, stating that any legitimate Sudanese government must include the main opposition coalition. However, General Burhan shifted blame to protest leaders for extending the crisis by refusing to agree on an interim government. The military and protest leaders had previously agreed on forming a transitional government for three years before elections, but negotiations stalled. The U.N. Security Council is set to discuss the Sudan crisis in a closed-door meeting on Tuesday. Monday's operation targeted the protest site near the Defense Ministry, where demonstrators had been gathered since April demanding civilian rule. Forces in police and military uniforms used batons, heavy gunfire, and explosions to clear the area, with videos showing protesters being beaten. Witnesses reported that hospitals were surrounded by paramilitary units. By mid-afternoon, the area was emptied. Military spokesman Shams El din Al Kabashi claimed the forces only acted against 'dangerous groups' within the protest camp. The Alliance for Freedom and Change called on protesters to 'continue the revolution,' leading to road blockades in Khartoum. They also demanded justice for security forces involved in the killings.

El general Abdel Fattah al-Burhan declaró en un discurso transmitido por televisión que un nuevo gobierno será formado de inmediato, sin la participación de los grupos de protesta, y permanecerá en el poder hasta que se celebren elecciones bajo supervisión internacional dentro de los próximos nueve meses. La decisión del militar viene después del colapso de las conversaciones con la Alianza por la Libertad y el Cambio, una coalición de manifestantes y partidos de oposición. La Asociación de Profesionales Sudaneses describió el ataque del lunes como una 'masacre,' acusando a las fuerzas de seguridad de violencia indiscriminada. Tibor Nagy, el principal diplomático estadounidense en África, condenó duramente el ataque, declarando que cualquier gobierno legítimo en Sudán debe incluir a la principal coalición de oposición. Sin embargo, el general Burhan transfirió la culpa a los líderes de las protestas por extender la crisis al negarse a llegar a un acuerdo sobre un gobierno interino. El militar y los líderes de las protestas habían acordado previamente la formación de un gobierno transitorio durante tres años antes de las elecciones, pero las negociaciones se estancaron. El Consejo de Seguridad de las Naciones Unidas discutirá la crisis en Sudán en una reunión a puerta cerrada el martes. La operación del lunes se dirigió contra el sitio de protesta cerca del Ministerio de Defensa, donde los manifestantes se habían reunido desde abril exigiendo un gobierno civil. Las fuerzas vestidas con uniformes de policía y militar utilizaron porras, tiros intensos y explosiones para despejar el área, con videos que muestran a manifestantes siendo golpeados. Testigos informaron que los hospitales fueron rodeados por unidades paramilitares. A mediada la tarde, el área fue evacuada. El portavoz militar, Shams El din Al Kabashi, afirmó que las fuerzas solo actuaron contra 'grupos peligrosos' dentro del campamento de protesta. La Alianza por la Libertad y el Cambio instó a los manifestantes a 'continuar la revolución,' lo que llevó a bloqueos de carreteras en Jartúm. También exigieron justicia para los miembros de las fuerzas de seguridad involucrados en los asesinatos.

article_content: In 2013, the Westmore News covered the opening of a sluice gate at the Bowman Avenue Dam, a $2 million project aimed at reducing downstream flooding. Local politicians, including Rob Astorino, attended the unveiling, marking his first sluice gate event. However, the dam's systems were infiltrated by Iranian hacker Hamid Firoozi, who could have caused catastrophic damage if fully operational. Cybersecurity experts highlight the use of 'dorking' search engines to exploit vulnerabilities, a technique now increasingly used by malicious actors. This method involves advanced search functions to uncover sensitive information, posing significant risks to critical infrastructure. The article underscores the urgency for improved security measures to prevent future attacks.

article_content: United Nations peacekeepers have met with senior military officers from Ethiopia and Eritrea in a bid to calm rising tensions over their border dispute. The U.N.-created military commission met Monday, Nov. 21, in Kenya's capital, Nairobi, for the first time since the United Nations said earlier this month that the border situation had become 'tense and potentially volatile.' There was no immediate word on the outcome of the talks. The meeting came a day after U.N. officials said about 30 Ethiopian troops had briefly entered a demilitarized buffer zone along the border. Also Thursday, Eritrea rejected a U.N. Security Council resolution that threatens sanctions against Ethiopia and Eritrea if they use force to settle their border dispute. Rising tensions have heightened fears that the countries will repeat their 1998-to-2000 border war, which killed 70,000 people.

No hubo informes inmediatos sobre el resultado de las conversaciones. La reunión ocurrió un día después de que los funcionarios de la ONU informaran que alrededor de 30 tropas etíopes habían entrado brevemente a una zona desmilitarizada junto a la frontera. article_content: The box office hit 'The Help' won an Oscar for best supporting actress, yet Viola Davis, the film's lead actress, was overlooked. In fact, no African-American woman has ever won best actress in a leading role. This has highlighted the lack of award-winning roles for African-Americans, especially women. Hattie McDaniels was the first African-American to win an Oscar, but her role in 'Gone with the Wind' reinforced stereotypes. Playwright Murray Horwitz argues that many roles present African-Americans as victims. In 1991, Whoopi Goldberg won an Oscar for playing a psychic in 'Ghost,' but critics noted it played into stereotypes. Halle Berry became the first African-American to win an Oscar for best actress in 2001 for 'Monster's Ball.' Her role was seen as more nuanced, but Horwitz believes more diverse roles are needed. Despite progress, layered roles remain rare, and most fit traditional niches. Mo'Nique won an Oscar for her role as an abusive mother in 'Precious,' which some argue perpetuates negative stereotypes. Lee Daniels defends his film, stating it tells a necessary truth. Octavia Spencer won an Oscar for her role in 'The Help,' which she based on her mother. Halle Berry remains the only African-American woman to win best actress, raising questions about race-neutral roles in Hollywood.

article_content: ISTANBUL - Turkey's High Election Board denied a request by the ruling AK Party to recount all votes in 31 of Istanbul's districts, a board member revealed on Tuesday, dealing a significant blow to the party's push for a citywide recount. President Tayyip Erdogan, leader of the AKP, stated on Monday that the local elections were marred by 'systematic fraud' at ballot boxes in Istanbul, raising the possibility of redoing the March 31 vote in the city where the opposition narrowly took control. Erdogan's remarks, his strongest challenge yet to the election process in Turkey's most populous city, caused the lira to drop sharply and also impacted Turkish stocks. The AKP's representative on the election board, Recep Ozel, informed reporters after a closed-door meeting that the board had only approved a recount of 51 ballot boxes scattered across 21 districts. Each box holds several hundred votes. The AK Party had also demanded a full recount in Istanbul's Buyukcekmece district, but the board has yet to issue a decision on that request, Ozel added. Recounts are ongoing in other districts. Main opposition candidate Mansur Yavas, now confirmed as Ankara's mayor, received his certification from election board head Bahattin Ozbas on April 8, 2019. Erdogan's AK Party has suffered losses in both Ankara and Istanbul. The party has governed both cities for 25 years. Erdogan argued that the extent of electoral irregularities uncovered by his party justifies nullifying the Istanbul mayoral election results, where the opposition's lead is less than 15,000 votes in a city of 10 million.

El presidente Tayyip Erdogan, líder del AKP, declaró el lunes que las elecciones locales habían sido afectadas por 'fraude sistémico' en las urnas de Estambul, lo que plantea la posibilidad de repetir la votación del 31 de marzo en la ciudad, donde la oposición obtuvo una estrecha victoria. Las declaraciones de Erdogan, su mayor desafío hasta la fecha al proceso electoral en la ciudad más poblada de Turquía, causaron una fuerte caída de la lira y también afectaron a las acciones turcas. El representante del AKP ante el tribunal electoral, Recep Ozel, informó a los reporteros después de una reunión a puerta cerrada que la junta solo había aprobado el recuento de 51 urnas electorales distribuidas en 21 distritos. Cada urna contiene varios cientos de votos. El Partido AK también había exigido un recuento total en el distrito de Buyukcekmece de Estambul, pero la junta aún no ha emitido una decisión sobre esa solicitud, según Ozel. Los recuentos de votos continúan en los distritos restantes. El principal candidato opositor de la capital, Mansur Yavas, habla con los medios después de recibir el documento que lo confirma como nuevo alcalde, de manos de Bahattin Ozbas, jefe de la junta electoral, en Ankara el 8 de abril de 2019. El partido AKP de Erdogan ha perdido la alcaldía de la capital Ankara ante el principal partido opositor, el Partido Republicano del Pueblo (CHP), y ha impugnado varios estadios del conteo en Estambul que mostraron una estrecha victoria de CHP. El AKP, con raíces islamistas, se recupera de la posible pérdida de ambas ciudades, que el partido y sus predecesores han gobernado durante un cuarto de siglo. Erdogan llegó a prominencia como alcalde de Estambul en la década de 1990 antes de convertirse en líder nacional. Erdogan sostuvo que el alcance de las irregularidades electorales que su partido ha descubierto justifica la anulación de las elecciones para la alcaldía de Estambul, donde la oposición aventaja por menos de 15,000 votos en una ciudad de 10 millones de electores.
